title: Data-driven estimation in equilibrium using inverse optimization
contribution: Poses the inverse variational inequality problem and, through a conic-duality characterization of approximate equilibria, estimates unobservable equilibrium primitives (utilities, congestion functions) as conic programs (parametric) or N-sized convex QPs (kernel, nonparametric) with generalization and prediction guarantees, shown on synthetic Bertrand-Nash and Sioux Falls Wardrop data.
problem_entry: Equilibrium primitives are unobservable while equilibria are observable, and errors matter most in redesign (p. 2); structural estimation needs a full parametric and probabilistic model and a non-convex GMM fit (p. 3), BLP-type methods need interior equilibria (p. 11); posed as an inverse VI, claimed first (pp. 3, 9). Domains DA + CP + ML, with AP (traffic, pricing) as testbeds.
key_idea: Theorem 2 (from Aghassi-Bertsimas-Perakis 2006): x is an eps-approximate equilibrium iff dual feasibility A^T y <=_C f(x) and a duality-gap bound hold; imposing it per observation with a common f gives one program whose class depends only on how f depends on theta (LP/SOCP for f linear in theta over nonlinear basis functions), and an extended representer theorem turns the minimum-RKHS-norm nonparametric fit into a convex QP sized by N (pp. 8-10, 15-16).
assumptions: VI over conic-representable sets with a Slater condition (A1-A2, pp. 8-9); Theta compact, f continuous in theta (p. 10); guarantees need i.i.d. data, a.s. Slater and feasibility, sets in a ball of radius R (A3-A6, pp. 20, 22), and strong monotonicity for prediction (Thm 8, p. 23); continuous problems only (p. 4); no partial derivatives of the unknown (Remark 4, p. 19); all data synthetic: Bertrand-Nash N = 250 and N = 40 with unobserved shocks and a misspecified class, Sioux Falls N = 40 with BPR flows and 10% perturbations (pp. 24-28).
proof_devices: Strong conic duality characterization of eps-approximate equilibria, plus a complementary-slackness variant (Thm 2, Eq. 10, pp. 8-9)
Observations as data: complexity set by the theta-dependence only (Remark 3, p. 10); LP for linear demand, non-convex for logit demand (pp. 11-12)
Representer theorem for the constrained multivariate case by orthogonal projection (Thm 4, p. 15; App. A.1, p. 31) and its general condition (§6, p. 18); finite convex QP (Thm 5, p. 16)
Dualizing the residual-norm constraint into a penalty to avoid infeasibility (Eq. 25, p. 16)
Ambiguity-set envelopes as LPs in (alpha, y) (§6.2, p. 19)
Scenario approach: the l-infinity fit as a randomized uncertain convex program with binomial-tail confidence (Thm 6, p. 20; App. A.3, p. 32)
Rademacher bound with an O(1/sqrt N) term and a duality-based uniform residual bound B (Thm 7, p. 22; Lemmas 1-3, pp. 32-33)
Prediction bound via Pang's error bound under strong monotonicity (Thm 1, p. 8; Thm 8, p. 23)
Low-rank kernel matrix and shortest-path decomposition for fixed coefficients (pp. 17-18)
Structural estimation recast as an inverse VI exposes bilinear non-convex terms (App. B, pp. 34-35)
experiments: Synthetic only; no solver, machine or run time reported. Bertrand-Nash: the parametric fit recovers the truth exactly, a CV-tuned Gaussian-kernel fit is equally exact but different, ambiguity band shown (pp. 24-25); misspecified case: theorem allows violation probability <= .21, observed .025, lambda reported as .01 and .1 (p. 26); kernel fit non-monotone, no prediction error (p. 27). Sioux Falls: degree-3 polynomial-kernel fit, mean relative approximation error 6.5%, prediction error about 5.5%, bound 9.73e5 vs CV 6.24e5 vs held-out 7.78e5 (pp. 28-29). No estimator baseline run (App. B is analytic only).
positioning: Generalizes inverse optimization (Heuberger, Ahuja-Orlin, Iyengar-Kang) from optima to equilibria and claims priority (p. 3); calls structural estimation complementary and shows equivalence with traditional estimators under interior equilibria (pp. 4, 34-35); sides with Breiman's algorithmic culture (p. 3); core device a self-citation (p. 8); learning theory borrowed (pp. 12, 20-21); Keshavarz-Wang-Boyd listed (ref. 29, p. 30) but not cited in the text of this version.
writing: Priority claim and predictive philosophy first (p. 3), five numbered contributions (pp. 4-5), remarks advertising strengths (p. 10), insights listed before the experiments (pp. 23-24), candid wording on recovery, CV and non-monotonicity (pp. 24, 26-27); one-paragraph conclusion without limits (p. 29); slips in this version: running head Berstimas, text vs Fig. 1 legend, lambda .01 vs .1 (pp. 2, 25-26).
limits_future: Stated: continuous problems only (p. 4); Thm 6 proof only for the l-infinity norm (p. 21); loose Rademacher bounds in small samples, use CV or bootstrap (p. 23); non-identifiability persists as N grows (p. 25); non-monotone kernel fits (p. 27); partial-derivative case left open (p. 19), the only future direction. Unstated: no real data, run times or estimator baseline.

method_links.note: Econometrics-owned estimation of equilibrium primitives written exactly as a conic program via a duality device; class kept (LP/SOCP for f linear in theta, convex QP for kernels); boundary printed (logit non-convex, partial derivatives, bilinear structural form). Also Tension T3: sold on minimal probabilistic assumptions, yet every guarantee rests on i.i.d. sampling and learning theory.
Data-driven and motivated by downstream design decisions, but scored only by approximation and prediction error on synthetic data; no owner, current rule or decision metric.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Duality-gap characterization makes inverse problems single convex programs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Approximate optimality or equilibrium per observation written as dual feasibility plus a gap <= eps; the observations become data, so the class depends only on the parameters.

Upper and lower envelopes of all kernel functions that reconcile the data (LPs), with kappa from a generalization bound or two CV standard deviations; shows that a well-identified parametric fit is one of many.
Fits a VI for predictive power with no claim to reflect the true mechanism; structural estimation called complementary, not wrong.

transferable: Characterize approximate optimality or equilibrium by dual feasibility plus a duality gap eps_j per observation, then minimize ||eps|| over the unknown parameters (pp. 8-10).
Parametrize the unknown map linearly in theta over nonlinear basis functions so the inverse problem is an LP or SOCP (p. 10).

Nonparametric version: minimum-RKHS-norm fit with a normalization constraint, reduced by a representer theorem to a convex QP in n*N coefficients; dualize the residual-norm constraint into a penalty (pp. 15-16).

Compute the envelope of all kernel functions within kappa of the best fit (one LP per evaluation point) before trusting a parametric form; set kappa from a generalization bound or two CV standard deviations (pp. 19, 22-23, 27, 29).
Tune hyperparameters by CV on half the sample and refit on the other half so a no-data-snooping theorem still applies; report theorem bound, CV and held-out estimates side by side (pp. 26, 28-29).
Exploit a low-rank kernel matrix and the shortest-path decomposition for fixed coefficients on network instances (pp. 17-18).

quotes.text: We make no claim that this fitted model accurately reflects “reality,” merely that it has good predictive power.
Calculating nonparametric sets of plausible alternatives helps guard against these types of unwarranted claims.

title: Robust queueing theory
contribution: Replaces renewal-process primitives with CLT/generalized-CLT-inspired polyhedral uncertainty sets, derives closed-form worst-case system-time bounds for possibly heavy-tailed multi-server FCFS queues, proves that departures (with adversarial servers), superposition and thinning stay in the set family so networks decompose, and after regression calibration of the variability parameters approximates simulated network system times (RQNA) with mostly single-digit percent errors, ahead of QNA on Kuehn's network.
problem_entry: GI/GI/m analysis is largely intractable (Pollaczek; his own 1990 method needs a 4.5-million-dimensional system for p = 5), networks lose Burke's theorem, simulation is slow for heavy tails, QNA/QNET miss heavy tails (pp. 2-3); Kingman's doubt about random arrivals as authority (p. 3); posed as worst-case analysis over uncertainty sets plus a network calculus (pp. 3-6). Domains SD + RO.
key_idea: Make the limit laws the primitives: bound partial sums of inter-arrival and service times by (n-k)/lambda - Gamma (n-k)^(1/alpha) and (n-k)/mu + Gamma (n-k)^(1/alpha) (polyhedral sets), take the worst case of the Lindley/Krivulin recursion (a one-dimensional problem with a closed form), show the family is closed under departure, superposition and thinning, and calibrate Gamma on simulated single queues so the worst case approximates the mean (pp. 7-13, 25-49).
assumptions: Single-class FCFS m-server queues with rho < 1 (p. 11); Assumption 1 sets with 1 < alpha <= 2, symmetric tails in §§3-5, asymmetric in §6 (pp. 9-11, 42); sets imply bounded service times, not independence (p. 10); adversarial servers for departures (pp. 26, 36); rational thinning by a round-robin split (pp. 38-39); sub-stochastic routing (p. 42); simulated data with normal, truncated Pareto, Erlang and exponential distributions, n = 30,000 arrivals, Kuehn's nine-queue network and random 10-30-node networks (pp. 45-53).
proof_devices: Exchange of maximization order plus a constructed worst-case path with nondecreasing service times by backward substitution (Prop. 1, p. 12)
Reduction to a one-dimensional maximization over the index and a closed form via continuous relaxation, max beta x^(1/alpha) - delta x (Eqs. 12, 15, p. 13; Eq. 45, p. 24)
Tightness argument: error vanishes as rho -> 1 and for large n (p. 14; details in an appendix not in the file)
Restricted no-overtaking policy class, explicit recursion and induction showing the FCFS worst case equals it (Props. 2-4, pp. 15-24)
Departure set inside the arrival set via two-case arguments on concave g and h (Thm 4, pp. 28-33)
Superposition by a one-dimensional concave maximization over the arrival share plus induction; thinning by round-robin split and recombination (Thms 5-6, pp. 36-40)
Network fixed point made linear by the substitution x_j = (lambda_j Gamma_a,j)^(alpha/(alpha-1)) (Thm 7, pp. 40-42)
Comparison of the closed form with Kingman's bound (pp. 25-26)
experiments: Gamma fitted by linear regression on simulated single queues before any network (Table 1, pp. 45-46); single queues within about 9.5% (p. 47); Kuehn's network: QNA 5.84-23.71% vs RQNA 6.74-9.28% (service-independent) and 0.68-3.88% (service-dependent), one cell where QNA beats service-independent RQNA (5.84 vs 7.12), unremarked (Table 4, p. 50); multi-server up to 10.91% (Table 5, p. 51); random networks 2.72-8.64% (Tables 7-10, pp. 52-53). No run times, confidence intervals or instance counts; QNA only in Table 4.
positioning: Against the probabilistic tradition (Erlang, Pollaczek, Burke, Jackson, Kingman) and its approximations (QNA, QNET) (pp. 1-3); distinguished from deterministic and stochastic network calculus and adversarial queueing on assumptions, tightness and generality, quoting network-calculus critics (pp. 4-6); self-citations frame a Bandi-Bertsimas programme and data-driven sets (pp. 2-4, 48); QNA chosen as the benchmark (p. 49).
writing: Historical introduction and a Kingman authority quote (pp. 1-3); 'in our opinion' on RO (p. 3); contributions (a)-(f) by section (p. 6); insights after each main result (pp. 25, 33, 41, 44); claims exact performance analysis of the stochastic system (p. 4) though matching needs regression calibration (pp. 45-47); headline error figures drift: single digits (pp. 1, 53), often 4-6% and at most 8% (p. 5), within 8.7% (p. 43), below 8.5% (p. 52), vs 10.91% and 8.64% in Tables 5 and 10 (pp. 51, 53).
limits_future: Stated: closed forms nearly tight only in heavy traffic (p. 14); asymmetric-tail and superposition bounds not or maybe not tight (pp. 42-43); adversarial-server assumption (p. 36); sensitivity to diverse arrival distributions (pp. 1, 53); heavy tails truncated in simulation (p. 45). Future: transient analysis (companion paper) and priority disciplines (pp. 6, 53-54). Unstated: all numbers depend on simulation-fitted theta; no run-time comparison.

method_links.note: Queueing-owned performance analysis rewritten as worst-case optimization over polyhedral sets; tractability kept as closed forms, 1-D problems and a linear system, not a solver class; no dual reading; boundary printed only in part. Also Tension T3: probability supplies the sets (CLT/GCLT) and, via simulation regression, the parameters.

Gamma_a and Gamma_s are the knobs that limit the adversary and set the degree of robustness, but they are fitted by regression to simulated means rather than priced for a decision-maker: the knob set from data.
Unquantified why-now: commercial codes solve large structured LP/MIP/QP and RO is fast-growing; no speed-up figure, and the results need no solver except Fig. 1.

Incumbent approximation (QNA) as opponent, beaten on the one network where it is run; no exact solve or certificate; QNA absent from multi-server and random-network tables. Headline (single digits) vs 10.91% table entry: Tension T6.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: CLT and generalized CLT scaling (n-k)^(1/alpha) with quantile-like Gamma turned into polyhedral sets on partial sums of inter-arrival and service times.
Departures (adversarial servers), superposition and thinning map the set family to itself with explicit parameter maps, so each queue is analysed alone (robust Burke theorem).
Variability parameters fitted by regression on simulated single queues so that the worst-case system time approximates the expected one; then validated on networks.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Recover the incumbent theory's qualitative law first
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Closed-form bound shares Kingman's dependence on lambda/(1-rho) and variability/m before any numerical comparison.

transferable: Bound partial sums, not individual variables, with the CLT/GCLT scaling (n-k)^(1/alpha) and a quantile-like Gamma (pp. 7-10).
Exchange max and sup for an upper bound, then construct a feasible extremal path (nondecreasing service times by backward substitution) to show it is attained (p. 12).
Relax a discrete index to a continuous one for closed forms and state where the relaxation is tight (heavy traffic, large n) (pp. 13-14).
Solve a restricted policy class (no overtaking) exactly and prove the worst case over all FCFS behaviour equals it (pp. 15-24).
Reduce coupled nonlinear network equations to a linear system by a power substitution (pp. 41-42).
Calibrate a worst-case model on isolated components and validate it on systems never used in calibration (pp. 45-53).
Report errors along each axis a sceptic would vary: servers, network size, feedback, traffic intensity, distribution diversity (pp. 50-53).

quotes.text: The key idea of our approach is to make the limit laws of probability theory the primitive assumptions
In summary, the adaptation of the variability parameters allows a mapping of the expected system time obtained by simulations to the worst case system time under our approach.

title: The power of optimization over randomization in designing experiments involving small samples
contribution: Assigns small samples to experimental groups by an MILP that minimizes the worst pairwise discrepancy in means and second moments and then randomizes the treatment labels, showing via number-partitioning asymptotics and simulation exponentially smaller covariate discrepancy than randomization, pair matching, re-randomization or FSM, with a re-optimizing bootstrap test that gives more power in a simulated mouse tumour study.
problem_entry: A practitioner's problem: mouse oncology groups of 8-10 with tumour-size CV of 50% or more (p. 2); randomization leaves 0.66 SD discrepancy for four groups of ten and needs more than 400 per group for 0.1 SD (p. 3); block designs and pair matching do not fix continuous covariates in small samples (pp. 2-3). Domains IO + ML (design of experiments), AP (preclinical oncology).
key_idea: Replace random assignment by an exact MILP minimizing max over group pairs of mean discrepancy plus rho times second-moment discrepancy (four linear constraints per pair, symmetry broken by x_ip = 0 for i < p), then randomize which group gets which treatment to keep unbiasedness; test by a bootstrap that re-solves the assignment on each resample (pp. 4, 7-8).
assumptions: n = mk subjects with normalized pre-treatment covariates (p. 4); rho chosen by the researcher and fixed arbitrarily (pp. 4-5); higher moments not in the objective (p. 6); potential outcomes under SUTVA (endnote 3, p. 9); all data simulated: normal, uniform and 3-D normal covariates, and a Gomp-ex murine tumour model with effects 0, 50, 250 mg (pp. 3-8); no real experiment.
proof_devices: MILP with m(1+2n-m)/2 binaries and one continuous variable; symmetry breaking undone by label randomization (p. 4)
Multivariate MILP with whitened covariates and matrices M, V of pairwise moment differences (pp. 4-5)
Reduction (rho = 0, m = 2) to balanced number partitioning: optimum exponentially small in k (Karmarkar-Karp; Karmarkar et al.; Mertens) vs 1/sqrt(k) for randomization by Jensen (p. 6)
Pair matching on uniform covariates: k^(-3/2) or k^(-1) orders (p. 6)
Unbiasedness from randomizing treatment identity; no omitted-variable bias (p. 7)
Variance reduction vs re-randomization under Morgan-Rubin's additive model, which the paper calls very restrictive (p. 8)
Bootstrap test re-solving the assignment per resample (p. 8)
experiments: Gurobi v5.6, 8-core PC: n = 40, m = 4 to optimality in under 20 s, bound and incumbent plotted (p. 4); larger instances near-optimal in minutes, optimality proofs longer, no gaps reported (p. 4). Versus randomization, Mahalanobis pair matching, re-randomization (5%) and FSM: about 0.0005 SD vs 0.66 SD for four groups of ten (pp. 5-6, decoded); subjects per group for 0.1 SD: 3 / 128 / 9 / 4 (Table 1, p. 6); non-optimized moments similar, with pair matching better on 3rd and 5th moments at k = 10, 20 (decoded Table 2, p. 7); tighter estimates and higher rejection rates in the tumour study (Figs. 5-6, pp. 8-9); number of draws not stated; no real data.
positioning: Against Fisher's block designs, pairwise matching (Rosenbaum-Rubin; Greevy et al.), re-randomization (Morgan-Rubin, recast as principled cherry-picking) and Morris's FSM (pp. 2-3, 8-9); theory from probabilistic analysis of number partitioning (p. 6); general theory left to Kallus (2014), which reads all designs as minimizing worst-case variance (Heuristic 1 pointer) (p. 5); 17 references, none on covariate-adaptive allocation (p. 10).
writing: Slogan title; abstract with orders of magnitude and exponential claims (p. 2); one running example (four groups of ten mice) for problem and fix (pp. 3, 5-6); strong verdicts (starkly superior; benefits clear) beside admitted arbitrary choices (pp. 5, 8); caveats in endnotes (p. 9); closing extends to many fields and to Microsoft Excel (p. 9); nine printed pages, no theorem-proof structure; p. 9 says higher moments no worse than other methods, p. 6 more carefully says similar.
limits_future: Stated: optimality proofs slow for larger instances (p. 4); higher moments and interactions not optimized and may drive effects (pp. 6, 8); gains depend on the treatment effect (p. 8); bootstrap test possibly conservative (endnote 5, p. 9). Unstated: no real experiment or field use, no rule for rho, no certification status for the simulated solutions. No future-work section.

method_links.note: A statistics-owned design problem, settled by randomization since Fisher, written exactly as an MILP and extended to covariate vectors; boundary printed only qualitatively (optimality proofs slow for larger instances). Also Tension T3: the case rests on probabilistic analysis and a bootstrap test.

One joint MIO replaces an unoptimized practice; solver, version, machine and time stated; incumbents dueled on synthetic data with known truth. Deviations: no warm start, no gaps for larger instances; wins on means and variances, not on higher moments (Table 2 vs the p. 9 summary).

Owner and problem from practice (a Vertex scientist; mouse oncology), the current rule (randomization) as baseline, scored by decision-relevant power to detect a drug effect (missed rejections as squandered experiments); no field test.
rho is the knob between first- and second-moment balance; achievable range shown as rho varies (Fig. 4), then rho fixed arbitrarily, matching the SKILL's correction that knobs get fixed arbitrarily.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Optimize the partition, randomize the labels
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Groups are optimized, then treatment identities are shuffled, which keeps unbiasedness and undoes the symmetry-breaking constraint.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Re-solve the optimization inside the bootstrap
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Randomization tests do not apply to optimized assignments, so each bootstrap resample is re-assigned optimally to build the null distribution.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Verifiability as an argument for optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A reproducible optimum can be checked and any manipulation would worsen it, whereas no grouping can be verified as a true random draw.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Price the gap with the probabilistic analysis of the underlying combinatorial problem
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Balanced number partitioning results give an exponentially small optimum against 1/sqrt(k) under randomization; translated into subjects needed per group.

transferable: MILP for balanced assignment: minimize d with d >= +/-(mu_p - mu_q) +/- rho (sigma2_p - sigma2_q) for all group pairs, assignment and size constraints, and x_ip = 0 for i < p (p. 4).
Whiten multivariate covariates by the inverse square root of the sample covariance before balancing (p. 4).
Randomize treatment labels after optimizing the groups to keep the effect estimate unbiased (pp. 4, 7).
Bootstrap test for optimized designs: resample covariates, re-solve the assignment, recompute the effect, p = (1 + count at least as large)/(1 + B) (p. 8).
Report subjects per group needed for a target discrepancy for every method (Table 1, p. 6).
Check balance on moments outside the objective (higher, log, cross moments) against every competitor (Tables 2-3, p. 7).
Score a design by downstream inference (estimate spread, rejection rates at zero, small and large effects) under a mechanistic simulator (p. 8).

quotes.text: Indeed it does better because any manual manipulation of the optimized results would make the result less well matched than the reproducible optimum, which is verifiable, whereas no one grouping can ever be verified as the true result of pure randomization.
In a sense, the complement of this rate is the fraction of experiments squandered in pursuit of an effective drug.
